clue.text: Both comrades sadly out of action

indicators.note: sadly suggests things have gone wrong, so the letters of both comrades are knocked into a new order

explanation.surface: Two comrades, both regrettably laid up and unable to take part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sadly' rearranges the twelve letters of BOTH COMRADES.
explanation.definitionFit: A French phrase used in English for someone disabled or put out of a fight, literally outside combat.

clue.text: Maybe maidens, getting passionate, went too far

parts.note: a maiden in cricket is an over with no runs scored, so maidens are an example of overs
hot can mean passionate or ardent

explanation.surface: Young women carried away by passion overstepped the mark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' flags an example: in cricket a maiden is an over (a set of six balls) from which no runs come.
explanation.definitionFit: To overshoot is to go past a target or limit, i.e. to go too far.

clue.text: Attractively thin in general

definitions.meaning: Field Marshal William ... was a celebrated British general of the Burma campaign

explanation.surface: A remark that people are generally pleasingly slender.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is a link; 'general' is not the everyday adjective but a noun: Bill Slim commanded the British Fourteenth Army in Burma in the Second World War.
explanation.definitionFit: Slender in an attractive way is a standard dictionary sense; the second is a proper name of a famous military commander.

clue.text: English politician vigorous, putting out line expressing fellow-feeling

parts.note: MP, Member of Parliament

indicators.note: putting out means expelling, so one letter is taken away from the word for vigorous

parts.note: athletic means physically vigorous

explanation.surface: An energetic English politician shows sympathy by dropping a party line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'putting out' removes L from ATHLETIC, leaving ATHETIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Being able to share and understand another's feelings is the core sense of the adjective, a synonym for sympathetic.

clue.text: Bird with round part, one concealed

parts.note: a round shape is like the letter O

indicators.note: concealed means hidden inside, so the numeral goes within the word for part

parts.note: a role is an actor's part
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A bird with a rounded patch of plumage, one tucked out of sight.
explanation.walkthrough: As first printed the clue read 'yellow' (OR in heraldry), which gives a spare R; the corrected 'round' gives O. 'concealed' puts I inside ROLE.
explanation.definitionFit: The golden oriole is a bright yellow and black songbird, so it is an example of a bird.

clue.text: A daughter in shout of acclaim shows bluster

indicators.note: in places the article and the daughter's letter inside the cry of acclaim

parts.note: bravo is a cry of approval at a performance

explanation.surface: Someone cheered by applause starts to swagger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts A and D inside BRAVO.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean a boastful show of boldness meant to impress.

clue.text: One's opponents in a land beyond?

definitions.meaning: the team or faction one is against
the world after death, the hereafter

explanation.surface: A musing that one's enemies live in some distant land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is a link between the two senses; the question mark flags the euphemism for the afterlife.
explanation.definitionFit: Opposing parties are a common idiom; the phrase is also a euphemism for the realm of the dead.

clue.text: Scrutiny of nasty loveless voyeurs

indicators.note: nasty suggests something spoilt and messed up, so the remaining letters are jumbled
loveless means without love, which in tennis scoring is zero, the letter O, so one O goes

explanation.surface: An examination of unpleasant peeping toms who have no love in their lives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loveless' drops O (love as nil in tennis) from VOYEURS, giving VYEURS; 'nasty' rearranges those six letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A survey is a close examination or inspection, so it is a synonym for scrutiny.

clue.text: Fellow producing article in Paris about our country

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the French article goes around the country

parts.note: le is the French masculine definite article
UK, the United Kingdom, from a British newspaper's view

explanation.surface: A man writes a French article about Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fellow' here is just a man's first name, the gospel writer's, not a colleague or academic.
explanation.definitionFit: A man's first name stands for any male person, a crossword-only use of fellow.

clue.text: Involve troublemaker, one Conservative entering after time

parts.note: an imp is a mischievous troublemaker

indicators.note: entering means going into, so the pair of letters slot inside the word for after time

parts.note: late means after the due time
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Accuse a mischief-maker, a Tory who turned up late.
explanation.walkthrough: 'entering' puts I and C inside LATE, giving LICATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To implicate someone is to show them to be involved in a crime, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: What Lothario leaves behind? He's rat, possibly!

parts.note: the second word of the solution, once broken (rearranged), spells out these two clue words

explanation.surface: A seducer's trail of damage, blamed on a rat of a man.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as wordplay: HEARTS 'broken' gives HE'S RAT; 'possibly' admits it is one of several arrangements.
explanation.definitionFit: A Lothario is a womaniser, who leaves jilted lovers grieving behind him.

clue.text: Minister of religion is beginning to embrace change

parts.note: Rev, short for Reverend, a clergyman's title

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter, here of embrace

explanation.surface: A clergyman is starting to accept new ideas.
explanation.definitionFit: To revise is to alter or amend, so it is a synonym for change as a verb.

clue.text: Loyalist to begin tackling man and wife

indicators.note: tackling means taking on or grappling, so the verb for begin wraps around the couple

parts.note: to start is to begin
Al is a man's name

explanation.surface: A faithful supporter about to take on a married couple.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tackling' looks like football but means grappling with, i.e. holding the couple inside; 'and' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A stalwart is a staunch, dependable supporter, so a loyal adherent.

clue.text: Worker on field has nasty dung on arms

indicators.note: nasty suggests a messy state, so the letters of the following three words are jumbled

explanation.surface: A labourer on a sports pitch ends up with muck on his arms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nasty' rearranges DUNG ON ARMS; 'has' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A groundsman maintains a sports pitch or field, so he is a worker on one.

clue.text: Essential lodger, type who can type

parts.note: key means vital or essential
a boarder pays to live and eat in someone's house

explanation.surface: An indispensable lodger who also happens to be a typist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'type' appears twice: the first means a kind of person, the second the verb for using a keyboard.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who enters text on a keyboard is a person able to type.

clue.text: Model to disapprove of, not given work

indicators.note: not given means withheld, so the letters for work are taken out

parts.note: to oppose something is to be against it
op, short for opus, a musical work

explanation.surface: A fashion model is criticised for not being offered a job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not given' removes OP from OPPOSE.
explanation.definitionFit: To model for an artist is to sit or stand still in a set position, the verb sense.

clue.text: Quiet worker is devoted to a cause

parts.note: P, piano, the musical direction for quiet
an artisan is a skilled manual worker

explanation.surface: A silent craftsman is committed to a movement.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective it describes someone strongly committed to a party or faction.

clue.text: Observe one in a bar?

definitions.meaning: a bar of music contains several musical sounds written on the stave

explanation.surface: Watch out for someone drinking in a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: The bar is a measure of music, not a pub; the question mark signals that twist.
explanation.definitionFit: To take notice of is one sense; the other is a single written sound in a musical score.

clue.text: Lever altered, made loose

indicators.note: made loose suggests the letters are freed and allowed to fall into a new order

explanation.surface: A lever has been changed and slackened.
explanation.walkthrough: 'altered' looks like the anagram signal but is the fodder; 'made loose' rearranges it.
explanation.definitionFit: A treadle is a foot-operated lever that drives a machine such as a sewing machine.

clue.text: More than one celebrity is unreal — I'm knocked for six

indicators.note: a cricket phrase for being utterly overwhelmed, so the letters are sent flying and rearranged

explanation.surface: A celebrity finds fame unreal and feels utterly floored.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knocked for six' shuffles IS UNREAL and I'M together; in cricket a six is a hit clean over the boundary.
explanation.definitionFit: Luminaries are eminent, famous people, so the plural stands for celebrities.

clue.text: Fires created by one beginning to end

indicators.note: beginning to end tells you to shift the first letter to the back of the word for one

parts.note: single means one

explanation.surface: Blazes started by one person from start to finish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beginning to end' moves the S of SINGLE to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Ingle is an old word for a fire on a hearth, as in inglenook, so the plural means fires.

clue.text: Actress giving bishop a visit

parts.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
to call is to pay a visit

explanation.surface: An actress receives a clergyman on a visit.
explanation.definitionFit: Lauren Bacall was a Hollywood star, famous for films with Humphrey Bogart.

clue.text: Stones thrown by mere lads

indicators.note: thrown suggests the letters are tossed about into a different arrangement

explanation.surface: Mere boys are hurling rocks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'thrown' rearranges MERE LADS; the stones are gems, not missiles.
explanation.definitionFit: Emeralds are green precious gems, an example of stones in the jewellery sense.

clue.text: Maybe worker on paper pursuing beast is presented dramatically

indicators.note: pursuing means following behind, so the newspaper worker comes after the animal

parts.note: a stag is a male deer
ED, an editor, is an example of a newspaper worker

explanation.surface: A journalist chasing a wild animal makes a show of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' flags the editor as just one example of a worker on a newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: A play that is staged has been put on as a theatrical production.

clue.text: Lose temper with little son needing sleep

parts.note: S is the short form of son
a nap is a short sleep

explanation.surface: A parent gets cross with a child who needs a rest.
explanation.definitionFit: To snap is to speak suddenly and irritably, an idiom for losing one's composure.

clue.text: Socialists wanting fruit mostly and fish

parts.note: Reds is a slang term for socialists or communists

indicators.note: mostly means most of the word, so its last letter is dropped

parts.note: the almond is a fruit, a type of nut

explanation.surface: Left-wingers who want most of the fruit and some fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' cuts the last letter from ALMOND, giving ALMON.
explanation.definitionFit: The sockeye, a Pacific species, is also known by this name, so it is a kind of fish.

clue.text: Spies looking both ways

indicators.note: a word that reads the same in either direction can look both ways

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: Secret agents glance left and right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spies' is the verb, not the agents; the word reads the same forwards and backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To spy something is to catch sight of it, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Animal husband kept in nasty old pen running free

indicators.note: kept in means held inside, so the husband sits inside the rearranged letters
running free suggests the letters are let loose to scatter into a new order

explanation.surface: A beast's keeper is held inside a shabby enclosure while it roams loose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'running free' rearranges NASTY OLD PEN; 'kept in' places H inside that.
explanation.definitionFit: A breed of small hardy horse from the Scottish islands, so an example of an animal.
